messages.subject: Re: Refactoring vectors from std::vector to Eigen::Matrix
parts:
I guess I am probably the biggest proponent of tightening the connection between Stan and Eigen, but I don't know that there is anything that absolutely has to go into v1.1.2. The main things are

-- With a std::vector it is ambiguous as to whether the thing is going to be used as a vector in the linear algebra sense or just as a holder for some scalars. So, you have to actually read the code to find out. With Eigen, you have a pretty clear separation between Eigen::Matrix (or Eigen::Vector) and Eigen::Array and can tell it a glance whether the function is doing linear algebra stuff.

-- There are more (relevant) coefficient-wise operations defined for Eigen objects than for std::vectors. This link has many of them

http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/AsciiQuickReference.txt

Most of the STL operations (sorting, etc.) are not that common in statistical applications.

-- There is some scope for speed improvements with doubles, where Eigen does packetwise and Stan has been doing elementwise, that would also involve less code and scope for stupid bugs. Also, with -DNDEBUG we can turn off range-checking for accessing Eigen objects via (), which as far as I know can't be done with STL.

-- If mixed type operations ever get supported in Eigen (or we figure out how to make them work generally in Stan), then it would be good to have as much of Stan as possible using Eigen's idioms.

Ben

If we switched to Eigen::Matrix, wouldn't it be just as ambiguous? I don't think we're going to be able to tell whether a user wants an Eigen::Matrix vs an Eigen::Array.

Some of the difficulty we were having were with the reference LHS types of functions as well as reference argument types.

Can you help by pointing out exactly where the changes from std::vector to Eigen::Matrix would be useful? Once again, we're looking at the whole system, and maybe you can help narrow the focus down to something reasonable.

In our probability distributions, we're trying to vectorize anyway. As of right now, we can't really make use of the coefficient-wise operations. When implemented naively, you might be able to make use of Eigen functionality, but since we're trying to vectorize using templates to save us from writing thousands of versions of the same function, we're not really making use of it now. Less code is good. Stupid bugs bad. But I don't think turning off range checks is a good idea. Users are already tripping on indexing out of bounds. We're trying to give them the best error messages possible -- but if Stan just kicks for no apparent reason, I think it'll be even harder to debug. Besides, we should be testing index bounds in our code and we do except for the multivariate distributions. So I'm not sure what efficiency is to really be gained by turning off range-checking. I could be convinced otherwise, but I just think is just info on what could be done and not a real benefit for using Eigen.

Cool.

Ben, do you have any suggestions on learning how to use Eigen's expression templates? I'm reading through the documentation now, but it's pretty sparse. As an example, I want a function to return a reference to a row or column and be able to use that as a LHS in an expression. So although we can use it to do some of the manipulations, now the return type can't be used for reference operations as well as being passed into other methods expecting an Eigen::Matrix. Have any suggestions on how to deal with these sorts of issues? If you want to see where we're having this trouble, it's in assign() in stan/agrad/matrix.hpp (which depends on a few functions in both agrad/matrix and math/matrix). There are some tests in test/agrad/matrix_test.cpp for assign that flex the code in this way.

Perhaps if I really understood the expression templates, I'd be able to proceed a little quicker through the refactoring.

I think there are two issues here -- the Stan language
itself and how it's implemented under the hood. Let me
summarize some of the things I've said before.

Here's the typing lineup as I see it:

Stan Implementation
--------------------------------------------

real x; T;

vector[K] x; Matrix<T,Dynamic,1>
row_vector[K] x; Matrix<T,1,Dynamic>
real x[K]; vector<T>

matrix[J,K] x; Matrix,T,Dynamic,Dynamic>
real x[J,K]; vector<vector<T> >
vector[K] x[J]; vector<Matrix<T,Dynamic,1> >
row_vector[K] x[J]; vector<Matrix<T,1,Dynamic> >


real x[I,J,K]; vector<vector<vector<T> > >
vector[K] x[i,j];
...

I think the issue that confuses users is that there are
three ways to make a 1D object, four ways to make a 2D
object, four ways to make a 3D object, and so on.

As is, linear algebra's only defined on the Eigen types.

We could simply forbid 2D arrays, getting rid of these two types:

real x[K];
real x[J,K];

But I'd rather not eliminate the distinction between the
various kinds of Eigen objects. It follows the Eigen
implementation which specializes the class template of
Matrix for rows=1 (col vector) and columns=1 (row vector),
adding new operations.

Eigen itself also has an Array type, which could be used
to impelement both of the above types instead of
std::vector.

The big issue for me with the typing (and also for Eigen)
is that it allows us to tell what's going to happen with
operations like:

(row_vector,vector):scalar

or

(vector,row_vector):matrix

?

Changing the way all this works at this point would be
a pretty big undertaking. I'm just trying to change the
basic underlying type for the models, but I think I may
just back everything out -- the issue is that the parameters
get touched by a whole lot of the code base.

As far as efficiency goes, I don't think it's going
to make a measurable difference changing from std::vector<T>
to Matrix<T,Dynamic,1>. The big speed improvement comes
from vectorizing our auto-diff operations -- our time's all going
to computing gradients. You can see this
in the recent probability functions and in the new
matrix ops. The matrix ops will reduce to double-based ops
now.

Three things that will help with speed are:

-- basic Cholesky factor type
-- caching solutions for cov and corr matrices
-- vectorizing the Jacobian determinants for all
the transforms

I've been meaning to do the last two for a while now.

Moving to Eigen mixed types, even if we make it work, is
only a small part of the efficiency puzzle. If we got that
working, then we'd still have to vectorize. For that, we'd have
to vectorize in the right way to deal with the Eigen expression
templates, which is another enormous undrtkaing. Wherever Eigen
uses a matrix of var (that is, for any vector or matrix
containing parameters or transformed params or local variables
in a model), it's very inefficient to use that representation
directly. Some other basic data types for auto-dif might help,
but I've never been able to figure out how to make it work.

Whew -- didn't mean to go on that long.

- Bob

The most extensive thing is

http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/TopicInsideEigenExample.html
 
Ben

It depends on the data layout. The integer ops themselves
are relatively inexpensive and further, they can usually
be parallelized at the CPU level so that the time they add
to a bunch of double ops in the loop is zero.

If the data being looped over is local and you only do one
thing with it, then breaking it down into two loops can be faster.
If the data's not local and you do multiple things with it,
one loop can be faster. If the data's not local and you do only
one thing with it, it probably doesn't matter.

> Eigen partially avoids this situation with their expression templates, so that the compiler can write
> code that does multiple things with only one pass over the loop.

Most of the expression templates are to avoid
copying/allocating data. Doing multiple things in one
pass is a side effect. So it's more efficient if you're
doing

u = a * transpose(v) + w;

to not do the naive thing and allocate 3 new internal vectors
(1. transpose(v), 2. a * transpose(v), 3. a * transpose(v) + w)
and copy intermediate results into it, but to do the equivalent of:

for (n in 1:N)
u[n] = a * v[n] + w[n];

In some cases, Eigen will allocate intermediates to save
having to duplicate work, such as actually allocating a transpose
to do matrix multiplies so that you get better locality.
They use the traits to figure out when it's a win to allocate or not.

Agreed. With the caveat that it's never possible to
tell if a model's running properly because you can do
something like:

y ~ normal(0,1); z <- x[round(y)];

and whether the index is in range or not depends on an
unbounded random quantity y.

        functions that internally loop over the same length, it might be better for them to do one explicit loop with
        multiple
        operations inside.


    It depends on the data layout.  The integer ops themselves
    are relatively inexpensive and further, they can usually
    be parallelized at the CPU level so that the time they add
    to a bunch of double ops in the loop is zero.

    If the data being looped over is local and you only do one
    thing with it, then breaking it down into two loops can be faster.
    If the data's not local and you do multiple things with it,
    one loop can be faster.  If the data's not local and you do only
    one thing with it, it probably doesn't matter.


        Eigen partially avoids this situation with their expression templates, so that the compiler can write
        code that does multiple things with only one pass over the loop.


    Most of the expression templates are to avoid
    copying/allocating data.  Doing multiple things in one
    pass is a side effect.  So it's more efficient if you're
    doing

         u = a * transpose(v) + w;

    to not do the naive thing and allocate 3 new internal vectors
    (1. transpose(v), 2. a * transpose(v), 3. a * transpose(v) + w)
    and copy intermediate results into it, but to do the equivalent of:

       for (n in 1:N)
         u[n] = a * v[n] + w[n];

    In some cases, Eigen will allocate intermediates to save
    having to duplicate work, such as actually allocating a transpose
    to do matrix multiplies so that you get better locality.
    They use the traits to figure out when it's a win to allocate or not.


     >



                 -- There is some scope for speed improvements with doubles, where Eigen does packetwise and Stan has
        been doing
                 elementwise, that would also involve less code and scope for stupid bugs. Also, with -DNDEBUG we can
        turn off
                 range-checking for accessing Eigen objects via (), which as far as I know can't be done with STL.


             Less code is good. Stupid bugs bad. But I don't think turning off range checks is a good idea. Users are
        already
             tripping on indexing out of bounds. We're trying to give them the best error messages possible -- but if
        Stan just
             kicks for no apparent reason, I think it'll be even harder to debug. Besides, we should be testing index
        bounds in
             our code and we do except for the multivariate distributions. So I'm not sure what efficiency is to really
        be gained
             by turning off range-checking. I could be convinced otherwise, but I just think is just info on what could
        be done
             and not a real benefit for using Eigen.


        Range checking should be on by default, but the user should ideally be able to turn it off once it is verified
        that the
        model is running properly.


    Agreed.    With the caveat that it's never possible to
    tell if a model's running properly because you can do
    something like:

         y ~ normal(0,1);   z <- x[round(y)];

    and whether the index is in range or not depends on an
    unbounded random quantity y.

    For std::vector, the range-checking story is this:

        std::vector<double> x;

        double y = x[10];     // NO range checking

        double y = x.at <http://x.at>(10);  // YES range checking


    We use x[10] throughout, so we just need to figure out how to
    turn off checking in Stan.

    For Eigen, we need to turn off their checking.  Are we doing
    that in the makefile?  We should be checking the ranges ourselves.

    - Bob

Yes,

http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/TopicCustomizingEigen.html

gives examples such as

Here is an example of an extension file for adding methods to MatrixBase:

 MatrixBaseAddons.h


inline Scalar at(uint i, uint j) const { return this->operator()(i,j); }

inline Scalar& at(uint i, uint j) { return this->operator()(i,j); }

inline Scalar at(uint i) const { return this->operator[](i); }

inline Scalar& at(uint i) { return this->operator[](i); }


inline RealScalar squaredLength() const { return squaredNorm(); }

inline RealScalar length() const { return norm(); }

inline RealScalar invLength(void) const { return fast_inv_sqrt(squaredNorm()); }


template<typename OtherDerived>

inline Scalar squaredDistanceTo(const MatrixBase<OtherDerived>& other) const

{ return (derived() - other.derived()).squaredNorm(); }


template<typename OtherDerived>

inline RealScalar distanceTo(const MatrixBase<OtherDerived>& other) const

{ return internal::sqrt(derived().squaredDistanceTo(other)); }


inline void scaleTo(RealScalar l) { RealScalar vl = norm(); if (vl>1e-9) derived() *= (l/vl); }


inline Transpose<Derived> transposed() {return this->transpose();}

inline const Transpose<Derived> transposed() const {return this->transpose();}


inline uint minComponentId(void) const  { int i; this->minCoeff(&i); return i; }

inline uint maxComponentId(void) const  { int i; this->maxCoeff(&i); return i; }


template<typename OtherDerived>

void makeFloor(const MatrixBase<OtherDerived>& other) { derived() = derived().cwiseMin(other.derived()); }

template<typename OtherDerived>

void makeCeil(const MatrixBase<OtherDerived>& other) { derived() = derived().cwiseMax(other.derived()); }


const CwiseUnaryOp<internal::scalar_add_op<Scalar>, Derived>

operator+(const Scalar& scalar) const

{ return CwiseUnaryOp<internal::scalar_add_op<Scalar>, Derived>(derived(), internal::scalar_add_op<Scalar>(scalar)); }


friend const CwiseUnaryOp<internal::scalar_add_op<Scalar>, Derived>

operator+(const Scalar& scalar, const MatrixBase<Derived>& mat)

{ return
CwiseUnaryOp<internal::scalar_add_op<Scalar>,
Derived>(mat.derived(),
internal::scalar_add_op<Scalar>(scalar)); }


Then one can the following declaration in the config.h or whatever prerequisites header file of his project:


#define EIGEN_MATRIXBASE_PLUGIN "MatrixBaseAddons.h"


So, I think users could slip in arbitrary functionality.

Ben
